doc.title: Al Gafa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2023

title: The origin of 'Barcelona' and Dizzy adopting it
summary: He tells how his favorite composition grew from open-string voicings, Getz's missed chance, and Dizzy liking the chord.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well the tune that’s on that Pablo record, “Barcelona” it’s so listenable. It’s — and when you mentioned your composing often times comes from practicing I can almost picture
how that might happen, that you’re doing some technique thing on a chord and then you find yourself playing this other chord.
Now it needs a release. And — lovely.

Thank you. You know what? That happens to be my favorite composition. And I got only one bad break on it. Stan Getz wanted to record it. And Stan said, “Give me the music, I’ll record it.” So I gave him the music and then two months later he passed away. But I would have loved to have him record it because he had all those records with Chick Corea and this tune was — it was the both of them together. And that’s what — I would have loved to have him do that. And it’s been recorded by Al Haig and I think Steve Kuhn and you know, me and Dizzy. It’s my favorite composition. And it was created exactly what you said before. I tune my bottom string to a D, which is like a whole tone below the standard tuning. And I always play with it like that. And I’m using the three open strings on the bottom and they’re vibrating constantly on the bottom ‘cause I’m striking them and then I’m changing the voicings on the top. And so this thing just started with like a D major to a D minor to an E major to a G minor, you know it’s just like moving down and it just felt so good to play. And so there’s a continuation of this story. When I finally got it all together, even the bridge has the same bass pattern. The bass pattern is completely the same throughout the tune except for one little vamp. But it’s still the open D and A in the bottom. It’s just — I hate to say it but it’s a really good tune. So we were on the road, we were doing a tribute to Charlie Parker, which — with Billy Eckstine and Jay McShann and Earl Hines, you know they had their bands together. It was supposed to be a tribute to Charlie Parker but — with Billy Eckstine singing his hits was not, no longer a tribute to Charlie Parker. That was — Phil Woods was supposed to be on it but Phil left because of Billy’s selection of material. He didn’t want to be part of that. So in the — we’re sitting in the dressing room and Dizzy and I started playing and we get to this — it’s an E chord with a D in the bottom. Dizzy said, “What’s that chord?” So I told him what it was and I spelled it out and he heard it. And that’s the thing I think that got him interested in the tune and then we started, we rehearsed it and it became part of the repertoire.
